gist: Visitor asks a shop owner how many people work for him, and the owner answers about half, reading 'work' as actually doing work.

characters.looks: middle-aged man, casual jacket, friendly curious smile
shop owner, shirt and vest, weary resigned expression

wordplay.explanation: 'arbeiten bei Ihnen' means both being employed there and actually doing work; the owner answers the second sense.

ru.note: Russian 'сколько у вас работает' carries the same double meaning.

en.note: 'How many people work here?' keeps the double meaning.

gist: Pathologists at work are said to play a memory card game with muscles, punning on the term muscle memory.

characters.looks: pathologist in scrubs, gloves, mask, morgue apron

wordplay.explanation: 'Memory' is the German name of the matching card game; 'Muscle Memory' is also the term for motor memory, implying a game played with body parts.

cultureRefs: 'Memory' as the German brand name for the Concentration card game

ru.note: Memory game less known; need a Russian pun on 'мышечная память' or a known card game.

en.note: Memory game and 'muscle memory' both exist in English.

gist: Mother rejecting every suitor tells her daughter to marry a soldier, since soldiers make beds, sew buttons, cook and are used to obeying orders.

characters.looks: middle-aged woman, cardigan, knowing practical expression
young woman, ponytail, thoughtful and unsure
young soldier in uniform, neat, saluting obediently

gist: Riddle asks what is red and lies in the field, answered with a farmers' proverb whose German name also reads as an old farmer's menstrual period.

wordplay.explanation: 'Bauernregel' means a farmers' weather proverb, but 'Regel' alone also means menstrual period, so 'old farmer's period'.

gist: [2 jokes] Skydiving is compared to oral sex from a toothless grandma: both are great fun as long as you do not look down.

characters.looks: toothless elderly woman, grey bun, cardigan

gist: Drunk man making tea asks his wife whether lemons have little feet, revealing he squeezed the canary into his tea.

characters.looks: tipsy man, messy hair, red nose, pajamas
sleepy woman in nightgown, hair curlers
small yellow canary bird

gist: Origin story of the Christmas tree angel: a stressed Santa was asked by the angel where to put the tree and told it where to stick it.

characters.looks: stressed Santa, red suit, white beard, frazzled expression
small cheerful angel, white robe, halo, wings

cultureRefs: Western tradition of an angel topper on the Christmas tree

ru.note: Russian New Year trees usually have a star on top; show the angel topper clearly.

gist: Man with two left feet asks a shoe shop for flip-flips, twisting the word flip-flops to mean two identical shoes.

characters.looks: ordinary man, awkward stance, two left feet
shoe salesman, polo shirt, puzzled look

wordplay.explanation: 'Flip-Flops' altered to 'Flip-Flips' to suggest a pair of two matching left shoes; also plays on the idiom 'two left feet'.

en.note: Flip-flops and 'two left feet' both exist in English.

gist: A good parachute lasts five to ten years, a bad one lasts the rest of your life, because that life ends on the first jump.
French tanks have rear-view mirrors so the drivers can also see the front, mocking the stereotype of French retreat.

characters.looks: French tank driver, beret, helmet, nervous

wordplay.explanation: 'Front' means both the forward direction and the battle front, which the retreating tanks see only behind them.

cultureRefs: Stereotype of French military surrender in WWII

ru.note: 'Фронт' keeps the double meaning; the French-retreat stereotype is less familiar in Russia.

gist: Speaker cannot recommend a waxing studio because they got ripped off there, both overcharged and stripped of hair.

characters.looks: person with reddened skin, grimacing, holding receipt

wordplay.explanation: 'abgezogen' means both cheated/ripped off and pulled off, like wax strips.

ru.note: Russian 'меня там ободрали' has the same double meaning.

en.note: 'I got ripped off' keeps both meanings.

gist: If a consumer testing agency rated vibrators, would the grade 'satisfactory' beat 'good', since satisfying is the point.

wordplay.explanation: 'befriedigend' is a mediocre test grade (satisfactory) and also means sexually satisfying.

cultureRefs: Stiftung Warentest, German consumer product testing agency with school-style grades

ru.note: Russian grade 'удовлетворительно' works; replace Stiftung Warentest with Роскачество.

en.note: Use Consumer Reports or Which? and 'satisfactory' vs 'good'.

gist: Child teased for a long nose is consoled by the mother that the face just sits further back than other people's.

characters.looks: small child, very long nose, sad face, school backpack
warm mother, apron, comforting smile

gist: Someone says another's know-it-all attitude is the nail in their coffin, and the know-it-all corrects that coffins use screws, proving the point.

characters.looks: exasperated man, hands raised, frustrated face
smug man, glasses, raised finger, lecturing

ru.note: Use the idiom 'последний гвоздь в крышку гроба'.

gist: Student asks a master why Europeans think all Asians look alike, and the man replies he is not the master the student thinks he is.

characters.looks: young Asian martial arts student, training robe, earnest
elderly Asian man, robe, long white beard, embarrassed
elderly martial arts master, robe, white beard

gist: Son asks his father whether, when his feet fall asleep, he closes his corns, which in German are literally called chicken eyes.

characters.looks: curious young boy, big eyes, striped shirt
relaxed father in armchair, slippers, newspaper

wordplay.explanation: 'Hühneraugen' means corns on the feet but literally 'chicken eyes', so sleeping feet would close their eyes.

gist: Doctor's good news is that the left leg need not be amputated after all; the bad news is that the right leg should not have been amputated either.

characters.looks: doctor in white coat, clipboard, awkward smile
man in hospital gown, bandaged leg stump, hopeful

gist: Speaker tells the couch they want to be productive, and the couch, offended, 'leaves them sitting', an idiom for abandoning someone.

characters.looks: lazy person in sweatpants slumped on couch

wordplay.explanation: 'sitzen lassen' literally means leaving someone seated and idiomatically means abandoning or standing someone up.

ru.note: Needs a Russian couch pun, e.g. on 'не поддержал'.

en.note: Needs an English couch pun, e.g. 'it didn't support me'.

gist: Spoonerism contrasts falling asleep in a chair with soiling oneself in one's sleep, swapping the German word parts.

wordplay.explanation: 'im Stuhl einschlafen' (fall asleep in a chair) vs 'im Schlaf einstuhlen' (defecate in one's sleep); Stuhl means both chair and stool.

gist: Aphorism that it is better not to be taken seriously than to be taken by a man named Ernst, punning on the adjective and the name.

characters.looks: middle-aged man, mustache, suggestive grin

wordplay.explanation: 'ernst genommen' means taken seriously; 'von Ernst genommen' means taken (sexually) by a man named Ernst.

en.note: Could use 'taken earnestly' vs 'taken by Ernest'.

gist: The fastest way to burn 1000 calories is to forget a pizza in the oven, taking burning calories literally.

wordplay.explanation: 'burn calories' as exercise vs literally burning food.

ru.note: 'Сжечь калории' has the same double sense.

gist: Woman wants her two lovers' faces tattooed on her breasts, and the tattooist refuses because of the long faces they will pull in thirty years when the breasts sag.

characters.looks: young woman, confident, tank top, bold makeup
bearded tattoo artist, tattooed arms, outraged
two young men, smiling portrait faces

wordplay.explanation: 'lange Gesichter machen' means looking disappointed and also literally stretched faces on sagging breasts.

ru.note: Russian 'лица вытянутся' has the same double meaning.

gist: Scruffy unemployed man asks the job center for work, is offered an absurd dream job, asks if he is being mocked, and the clerk asks who started it.

characters.looks: greasy hair, tracksuit, slides, beer can, cigarettes
office clerk, glasses, tie, deadpan expression

cultureRefs: Adiletten slides as a slob stereotype

en.note: Jobcenter becomes job center or unemployment office.

gist: Photographer asks a model to pose nude, and she agrees but tells him to undress, flipping who gets naked.

characters.looks: man with camera, scarf, eager smile
fashion model, elegant dress, unimpressed look

gist: [2 jokes] Apprentice explains his boss died because the boss said when he nods his head, hit it, and he hit the head instead of the post.

characters.looks: young apprentice, overalls, sledgehammer, innocent face
craftsman foreman, work clothes, cap, holding post
curious man, casual clothes, concerned expression

wordplay.explanation: Ambiguous 'drauf' (on it) refers to either the post or the nodding head.

ru.note: 'Кивну головой — бей по ней' keeps the ambiguity.

en.note: 'When I nod my head, hit it' is a known English form.

gist: [3 jokes] Fake Bible trivia claims the first car was a Ford because Adam and Eve sinned continuously, punning on a German word for nonstop.

characters.looks: bearded man with fig leaf
long-haired woman with fig leaf, apple

wordplay.explanation: 'in einem Fort' (continuously) sounds like 'in einem Ford'; also 'mit Triumph' and 'widerfahren' read as 'wieder fahren'.

cultureRefs: Old Testament quotations in German phrasing

en.note: Use English Bible-car puns like 'in one Accord' or 'Plymouth Fury'.

gist: Father shark teaches his son to circle a surfer before attacking so the prey soils itself first and tastes better.

characters.looks: big grey shark, scarred fin, wise fatherly look
small young shark, eager, impatient
young surfer on board, wetsuit, terrified

gist: Told his fly is open, a man says he is on standby, implying sexual readiness.

characters.looks: man pointing, embarrassed smirk
confident man, open fly, cheeky grin

wordplay.explanation: 'Bereitschaft' means on-call duty and also being ready (sexually).

ru.note: Use 'я в боевой готовности' or 'на дежурстве'.

gist: One secretary found condoms in the boss's desk, a second poked holes in them, and the third suddenly feels sick, implying she is pregnant by the boss.

characters.looks: office secretary, blouse, gossipy expression
office secretary, glasses, mischievous grin, holding needle
office secretary, pale, hand on stomach
middle-aged boss, suit, smug

gist: Man orders 99 rolls, the baker suggests rounding up to 100, and the man asks who is supposed to eat all those.

characters.looks: ordinary man, shopping bag, serious face
baker, white apron, flour-dusted, cheerful

gist: One-eyed man asks a one-legged man how it is going, and he answers it depends how you see it, each line hitting the other's disability.

characters.looks: man with eye patch, friendly wave
one-legged man on crutches, wry smile

wordplay.explanation: 'Wie geht's' (how are you, literally how does it walk) said to a one-legged man; 'wie man's sieht' (how you see it) said to a one-eyed man.

ru.note: 'Как идут дела?' and 'Как видишь' keep both puns.

en.note: 'How's it going?' and 'As you can see' keep both puns.

gist: Yo-mama insult: your mother is so dumb she plugs a reversible USB-C connector in the wrong way.

characters.looks: confused woman holding USB cable

ru.note: Yo-mama format is less common in Russian but understood.

gist: Patient asks whether he may bathe with diarrhea, and the doctor says yes if he can fill the tub, reading 'with' as 'in'.

characters.looks: pale man clutching stomach, towel over shoulder
doctor in white coat, stethoscope, deadpan

wordplay.explanation: 'mit Durchfall baden' means bathing while having diarrhea or bathing in diarrhea.

en.note: 'Take a bath with diarrhea' keeps the ambiguity.

gist: Man offering a spare place because he is getting married on cup-final day turns out to be giving away his bride, not his ticket.

characters.looks: football fan in team scarf, groom suit underneath
bride in white dress waiting in front of church
friend in football jersey, holding tickets

cultureRefs: Bayern Munich vs Borussia Dortmund football rivalry

ru.note: Swap teams and church for local ones if needed.

en.note: Swap teams and church for local ones if needed.

gist: Two Celts in a snowstorm: one curses the damn cold, the other hears 'damn Celt' and retorts 'you too'.

characters.looks: Celtic warrior, braided beard, fur cloak, freezing
Celtic warrior, red hair, plaid cloak, snow-covered

wordplay.explanation: 'Kälte' (cold) sounds like 'Kelte' (Celt), so 'Scheiß Kälte' is heard as an insult.

gist: Speaker says they now work at McDonald's in a frying capacity, punning on a German word for an advisory role.

characters.looks: fast food worker, cap, apron, spatula

wordplay.explanation: 'bratende Funktion' (frying function) puns on 'beratende Funktion' (advisory capacity).

gist: Researcher of medieval maids calls himself a maid-researcher, punning on the German word for market researcher.

characters.looks: scholar with glasses, old books, tweed jacket

wordplay.explanation: 'Magd-Forscher' (maid researcher) sounds like 'Marktforscher' (market researcher).

gist: Acquitted defendant is upset because, expecting prison, he had already rented out his apartment for three years.

characters.looks: lawyer in suit, briefcase, puzzled
grim middle-aged man, rumpled suit, worried

gist: Man asks a pharmacist for cyanide without a prescription, shows a photo of his wife, and the pharmacist accepts it as a valid prescription.

characters.looks: tired middle-aged man, wallet in hand
pharmacist in white coat, glasses, stern then understanding
stern scowling woman in photo

gist: A restaurant on the moon has great food but no atmosphere, punning on ambience and air.

wordplay.explanation: 'Atmosphäre' means both restaurant ambience and the air envelope the moon lacks.

gist: Blonde found in India explains the employment office said her office was at the end of the corridor, confusing the word with the Ganges river.

characters.looks: blonde woman, business suit, briefcase, sunhat
local man in India, curious expression

wordplay.explanation: 'am Ende des Ganges' means at the end of the corridor (Gang) and at the end of the Ganges river.

gist: First-person story of answering the doorbell, told entirely with swapped halves of German compound words, ending with nobody at the door.

characters.looks: dazed man in house clothes, bump on head

wordplay.explanation: Compound words and verbs are scrambled (e.g. Treppe/Wetze, Kopf/Rammel), so the humor is entirely in German word swaps.

gist: Child asks father why he married mommy, and he turns to his wife saying even the children cannot understand it.

characters.looks: small curious child, pigtails, big eyes
tired father, cardigan, sly smirk
middle-aged woman, arms crossed, offended look

ru.note: Rename Ingrid to a local name.

en.note: Rename Ingrid to a local name.

gist: Eskimo asked where his igloo is realizes he left the iron on, implying it melted.

characters.looks: Inuit man in fur parka, hood, puzzled
Inuit man in fur parka, shocked face

gist: Grandma gives a bus driver peanuts every day because her bad teeth only let her suck off the chocolate coating.

characters.looks: sweet elderly woman, headscarf, handbag, plastic bag
bus driver, uniform cap, munching peanuts

gist: Farmer proposes settling a duck dispute with groin kicks, kicks the city hunter first, then concedes the duck before taking his own kick.

characters.looks: city man in new hunting gear, shotgun
burly farmer, overalls, rubber boots, sly grin
dead duck lying in farmyard

gist: Pun riddle: a mumbling mussel is a blend of mussel and mumble, and a sneezing one blends the German word for blue mussel with sneeze.

wordplay.explanation: 'Nuschel' mixes Muschel (mussel) and nuscheln (mumble); 'Niesnuschel' mixes Miesmuschel (blue mussel) and niesen (sneeze).

gist: Finland is said to be close because experts say 'sauna', which sounds like German for 'so near'.

wordplay.explanation: 'Sauna' sounds like 'so nah' (so close) in German.

gist: Bragging about biceps is called 'upper arm', which sounds like German slang for really pathetic.

wordplay.explanation: 'Oberarm' (upper arm) also reads as 'ober-arm', extremely poor or lame.

gist: One cow says moo, many cows make trouble, with the German plural of cow plus moo sounding like the word for effort.

characters.looks: spotted dairy cow, bell around neck

wordplay.explanation: 'Kuh macht Muh' vs 'Kühe machen Mühe': the umlaut turns moo into Mühe (effort, trouble).
